lead: Series resonance is the frequency in a series RLC circuit where the inductive reactance and the capacitive reactance have equal magnitude and cancel. The impedance becomes pure resistance, the current reaches its maximum, and the source voltage and current are in phase. This sharp frequency choice is used in radio tuners, intermediate-frequency filters, wireless receivers, and any circuit that must pick one band and reject others. It also matters in power systems, where unwanted resonance can amplify harmonic currents and overheat capacitors.
prereq: You need: the V-I relations of R, L and C, and phasors and impedance from sinusoidal steady-state analysis.

sections.h3: Reactance cancellation sets the resonant frequency

blocks.text: In a series RLC circuit the same current I flows through R, L and C. At a sinusoidal source frequency f, in hertz, the angular frequency is ω = 2πf in rad/s. The inductive reactance is X<sub>L</sub> = ωL and the capacitive reactance is X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(ωC). Both are in ohms. The series impedance is:

Here z is the series impedance in Ω; R is resistance in Ω; X<sub>L</sub> = ωL is inductive reactance in Ω; X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(ωC) is capacitive reactance in Ω; ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s; f is frequency in Hz; j is the imaginary unit.

At low frequency X<sub>C</sub> is large and X<sub>L</sub> is small, so the circuit looks capacitive and the current is small. At high frequency X<sub>L</sub> is large and X<sub>C</sub> is small, so the circuit looks inductive. At one frequency the two reactances are equal: X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>. They cancel in the impedance, leaving Z = R. The phase angle is zero, and the current I = V/R is the largest possible for a fixed source voltage V. This condition is series resonance.
Here ω₀ is resonant angular frequency in rad/s; f₀ is resonant frequency in Hz; L is inductance in H; C is capacitance in F.

At resonance the phasors V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> are equal in magnitude and opposite in phase: V<sub>L</sub> leads the current by 90°, V<sub>C</sub> lags by 90°. Their sum is zero, so the whole source voltage appears across R, which sets the current. Some syllabi call ω₀ the natural frequency of the circuit; the same ω₀ returns, with the damping ratio, in the transient response of second-order RLC circuits.

sections.h3: The resonance curve and half-power points

blocks.text: A plot of current against frequency peaks at f₀, where I₀ = V/R. Away from f₀ the net reactance grows and the current falls on both sides. The sharpness of that fall is set by the quality factor of the series circuit:
Here q is the quality factor, dimensionless; R is series resistance in Ω; L is inductance in H; C is capacitance in F; ω₀ is resonant angular frequency in rad/s.

Q is dimensionless. With the same L and C, a smaller R gives a larger Q and a narrower peak; it also raises the peak, because I₀ = V/R. The half-power points are the two frequencies f₁ and f₂ where the current falls to I₀/√2, about 0.707 I₀. There the power in R is half its maximum, because P = I²R. The bandwidth is BW = f₂ − f₁ = f₀/Q; the chapter on quality factor and bandwidth derives it.

At resonance X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub> = √(L/C), the characteristic resistance of the pair. Therefore Q = X<sub>L</sub>/R = X<sub>C</sub>/R. The figure plots the current of the worked example circuit with R = 10 Ω (Q = 10) and with R = 20 Ω (Q = 5): doubling R halves the peak from 1 A to 0.5 A and doubles the bandwidth from 159 Hz to 318 Hz.

At resonance the current is I = V/R. The voltage across the inductor is V<sub>L</sub> = I X<sub>L</sub> = (V/R) X<sub>L</sub>. Because Q = X<sub>L</sub>/R, this becomes V<sub>L</sub> = QV. The capacitor voltage has the same magnitude: V<sub>C</sub> = QV. The two voltages are 180° apart, so they cancel in the Kirchhoff voltage loop, but each one individually can be much larger than the source voltage. This is voltage magnification.
Here v<sub>L</sub> is rms voltage across L in V; V<sub>C</sub> is rms voltage across C in V; Q is the series quality factor, dimensionless; V is rms source voltage in V.

A series RLC circuit at resonance is called an acceptor circuit, because it accepts current from the source most easily at f₀. The same behaviour is called voltage resonance, because the voltages across L and C are magnified. The damping ratio ζ = R/(2ω₀L) = 1/(2Q) links this phasor picture to the transient response; the overdamped, critically damped and underdamped cases belong to second-order transient analysis.

figure.caption: Left: current against frequency for the worked example (L = 10 mH, C = 1 µF, 10 V). With R = 10 Ω the peak is 1 A at 1591.5 Hz and the half-power band is 159 Hz wide; doubling R to 20 Ω halves the peak and doubles the band. Right: at resonance V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> are each 100 V, ten times the source, and cancel.

spec.aria: Resonance curves of current against frequency for R equal to 10 and 20 ohms, with the half-power band marked, and a phasor diagram of V R, V L and V C at resonance.

examples.question: A series RLC circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF. A 10 V rms sinusoidal source is connected at the resonant frequency. Find f₀, Q, the bandwidth, and the rms voltage across the capacitor.
steps: Convert: L = 10 mH = 10 × 10⁻³ H, C = 1 µF = 1 × 10⁻⁶ F, V = 10 V rms.
At resonance Z = R = 10 Ω, so I = V/R = 10/10 = 1 A rms.

V<sub>C</sub> = I X<sub>C</sub> = 1 × 100 = 100 V rms. V<sub>L</sub> = I X<sub>L</sub> = 100 V rms too, 180° away from V<sub>C</sub>. Check: V<sub>C</sub>/V = 100/10 = 10 = Q, the voltage magnification.
Half-power currents: I₀/√2 = 0.707 A, reached at about f₀ ± BW/2 = 1512 Hz and 1671 Hz.
examples.answer: f₀ ≈ 1591.5 Hz, Q = 10, bandwidth ≈ 159.2 Hz, I = 1 A, and V<sub>C</sub> = V<sub>L</sub> = 100 V rms, ten times the source voltage.
examples.check:
import math
R = 10.0
L = 10e-3
C = 1e-6
V = 10.0
f0 = 1/(2*math.pi*math.sqrt(L*C))
Q = (1/R)*math.sqrt(L/C)
BW = f0/Q
w0 = 2*math.pi*f0
XL = w0*L
XC = 1/(w0*C)
I = V/R
VC = I*XC
print(round(f0, 1))
print(round(Q, 1))
print(round(BW, 1))
print(round(VC, 1))

traps: Do not set X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub> at an arbitrary frequency. The equality X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub> holds only at ω₀, so recompute both reactances whenever the source frequency changes.
In Q = ω₀L/R use ω₀ in rad/s, not f₀ in Hz. Using f₀ in place of ω₀ introduces a 2π error.
V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> cancel in the source loop, but each can be Q times the source voltage. Do not add their magnitudes as if they were in phase.
The half-power current is I₀/√2, about 0.707 I₀, not zero and not I₀. Half power means P/P<sub>max</sub> = 1/2.

At resonance the impedance is R, not zero. If R is very small, the ideal model predicts a very large current and very large V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub>; real coils and sources always add some resistance.

quiz.q: Define series resonance for an RLC circuit.
quiz.a: Series resonance is the frequency where X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>. The impedance becomes purely resistive, Z = R, and the source voltage and current are in phase.

quiz.q: Why is the current maximum at series resonance for a fixed source voltage?
quiz.a: At resonance the reactances cancel, so the impedance magnitude is the smallest possible value, R. With fixed V, I = V/R gives the maximum current.

quiz.q: A series RLC circuit has R = 5 Ω, L = 50 mH and C = 2 µF. Find f₀.
A series RLC circuit has R = 20 Ω, L = 5 mH and C = 0.5 µF. Find Q, f₀ and the bandwidth.
At series resonance the source is 10 V rms and both V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> are 200 V rms. Find Q and explain why KVL is not violated.
quiz.a: Q = V<sub>C</sub>/V = 200/10 = 20. The phasors V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> are 180° apart, so their sum is zero. KVL is satisfied because the source sees only V<sub>R</sub>, which equals 10 V rms.

quiz.q: In a series RLC circuit, R is doubled while L and C stay fixed. What happens to f₀, Q and bandwidth?
quiz.a: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) does not change. Q = ω₀L/R halves because R doubles. BW = f₀/Q doubles.

quiz.q: What are half-power points in a series resonance curve?
quiz.a: They are the two frequencies f₁ and f₂ where the current is I₀/√2 ≈ 0.707 I₀. At these points the power in the resistor is half its maximum value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Radio receivers use a tuned LC tank to select one station; a varactor diode changes C and moves f₀ electronically. Wireless power transfer and induction heating run at resonance to get large coil currents from a modest source. Power engineers detune capacitor banks to keep network resonances away from harmonic frequencies that can overheat capacitors.
